title: Concentration Inequalities and Martingale Inequalities: A Survey
abstractRaw: We examine a number of generalized and extended versions of concentration inequalities and martingale inequalities. These inequalities are effective for analyzing processes with quite general conditions as illustrated in an example for an infinite Polya process and web graphs.

title: Automating Reproducibility Checks Using Large Language Models
abstractRaw: Computational reproducibility checks are essential to scientific credibility, yet few published papers are ever independently verified, largely because manual checking is labor-intensive and time-consuming. We tested whether an agentic large language model (LLM) could perform computational reproducibility checks at scale. We benchmarked computational reproducibility checks performed by an LLM analyst (Claude Opus running in the Claude Code harness) against results from expert-led reproducibility audits in the social and behavioral sciences and found that LLM accuracy was comparable to that of human experts. Agentic LLMs can now perform high-quality reproducibility checks relatively cheaply, quickly, and easily, putting large-scale audits within reach for journals, granting agencies, organizations, and individual researchers.

title: Why don’t web survey panelists complete a survey? An analysis of response refusal and discontinuation
abstractRaw: Not all participants complete web surveys distributed by web research companies. Some refuse to participate in the survey, whereas others discontinue their responses. This study examined the extent of similarity in the reasons for refusal and discontinuation among research company panelists, as well as the associations between refusal and discontinuation and demographic information and sense of busyness. In Study 1, data from 500 participants from a research company were analyzed. In Study 2, data from 600 participants from a research company were analyzed. The results showed that a large number of surveys being distributed was associated with a higher response rate, and the importance of the factors of refusal and discontinuation varied across groups. The findings are discussed with reference to the leverage-salience theory.

title: How should Moral Motivation be Represented? The Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA)
authors: Paul McKee, Gregory Samanez-Larkin, Scott A. Huettel, Walter Sinnott-Armstrong
abstractRaw: Moral psychology has mostly asked which motives drive moral action, and rarely how moral motivation should be represented once several are active at once. Most theories represent it as a single dominant motive or as one continuum from bad to good. Both discard information: a person torn between strong competing motivations and a person who feels nothing occupy the same position. We argue that representational format is a testable empirical claim, not a modeling convenience, and propose the Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA), which represents moral motivation as four independent dimensions formed by crossing motivational direction (approach, avoid) with perceived moral valence (good, bad). MoMA does not specify which motives matter; it specifies the space in which they combine. We derive requirements for an adequate architecture, show that lower-rank representations necessarily collapse psychologically distinct states, and state predictions distinguishing MoMA from simpler alternatives.

title: Coordinated Psychological Intervention Ensembles Outperform Single-Mechanism Designs Across Societal Challenges
authors: Anandita Sabherwal, Danielle Goldwert, Madalina Vlasceanu, Elke U. Weber
abstractRaw: Behavioral science tends to seek the single most predictive explanation for behavioral phenomena and subsequently the most effective intervention for behavior change. Yet many consequential outcomes, from climate action to democratic attitudes, result from multiple psychological processes, raising the question of whether combining interventions that leverage different processes would prove more effective. Across a 13-intervention megastudy and a second, megastudy-informed experiment (Ns = 8,488 and 2,547 US adults; both quota-matched and preregistered) we test whether intervention ensembles—deliberate combinations of distinct psychological modules delivered together—can more effectively shape target behaviors and attitudes.  We test three principles for constructing such ensembles: 1) outcome optimizing ensembles (combining top-performing individual interventions), 2) mechanism coverage ensembles (covering key psychological drivers of the outcome), and 3) multi-level synergy ensembles (combining individual-, collective-, and system-level processes). Ensembles consistently outperformed their constituent single-mechanism interventions. In Study 1, relative to an informed control, the strongest ensemble increased climate policy support by 41.5% and donation by 43.0%. And in Study 2, the ensemble was significantly more effective than its components in reducing partisan animosity and strengthening democratic attitudes. The largest gains were achieved by multi-level synergistic ensembles that aligned processes across individual, collective, and systemic levels. LLM-assisted analyses of participant reasoning reveal that effective ensembles work by resolving complementary psychological barriers, not by simply providing more arguments. For complex societal challenges shaped by multiple barriers, interventions can achieve behavior change at greater rate and scale by designing coordinated intervention ensembles rather than by searching for the single best mechanism.

title: Legislative Inconsistencies in Defining Psychology Registration in the Criminal Code Act 1899 (Qld): Mandatory Reporting and Implications for Provisional Psychologists
abstractRaw: 2021 amendments to the Criminal Code Act 1899 (Qld) in Queensland to criminalise the non-disclosure to police of child sexual abuse (CSA) (s229BC) had consequential implications for the practice of psychology, particularly psychotherapy. Where patients make self-disclosures about current or historical CSA perpetrated against them by an adult when they were a minor (including historical CSA in a now adult patient), psychologists, like all adults in Queensland are required to report that to police, unless one of the “reasonable excuses” against disclosure applies. This paper discusses the wording in the Act with a focus on relevant reasonable excuses in the therapy context, and how the Act contains ambiguity in the application of the law to psychology trainees who are provisional, rather than student registrants under the national health practitioner regulatory scheme.
